## Introduction

Anthropogenic global changes such as land-use change, resource exploitation, climate change, invasive alien species, and pollution pose major and accelerating threats to biodiversity and ecosystem functioning [@Ipbes2019-sd]. These global change drivers do not act in isolation but occur simultaneously and often interact in complex ways so that their net impacts may exceed the sum of single drivers [@oliver2014interactions; @Komatsu2019-yr; @rillig2019role; @Speiser2022-st; @xue2024number]. Given these complexities, forecasting changes to biodiversity requires an understanding of the mechanisms underlying the multifactorial and interactive nature of anthropogenic global change drivers.

A growing literature suggests that different global change drivers can affect community biomass, plant community diversity and composition in grasslands through a similar underlying mechanism: changes in community biomass that shift the intensity and nature of the dominant plant-plant interactions [@borer2014herbivores; @li2024water; @klein2004experimental; @collins2022global]. For example, warming and nitrogen addition typically increase community biomass, which may lead to communities with taller, faster growing species leading to biodiversity loss due to competitive exclusion of subordinates species [@Alexander2015-gu; @Vandvik2020-hu; @wust2021interaction]. A few studies have explicitly shown that this increased competitive exclusion with increased biomass is for light [@eskelinen2022light; @hautier2009competition]. In contrast, grazing removes biomass [@frank2005interactive; @Bernes2015-yg], which can lead to increased diversity, particularly in more productive habitats [@Austrheim2001-nu; @frank2005interactive; @niedrist2009plant; @Bernes2015-yg; @borer2024planning; @proulx1998reversal]. Accordingly, grazing has been shown in some cases to reverse the effects of warming and nitrogen addition, thus preventing species loss [@kaarlejarvi2017herbivores; @klein2004experimental; @post2008opposing; @song2020grazing].

While these studies suggest that different global change drivers can modify the magnitude and nature of competition for resources, notably light, the hypothesis that their combined impacts are mediated through the same mechanism – i.e., changes in community biomass – has rarely been tested in a unified way. @white2014direct studied direct and indirect effects of different drivers on plant diversity in three temperate grasslands and identified shoot biomass as a key indirect driver of species loss in response to grazing and precipitation. @Vandvik2020-hu showed that complex interactions of temperature and precipitation change could be simplified by including the biomass of novel species as a proxy of plant-plant interactions. Building on these findings, we propose that we can generalize and unify the effects of multiple global change drivers on plant biodiversity by using community biomass as a *common currency*, integrating the underlying impacts of these drivers on the intensity and outcome of plant-plant interactions for limiting resources (@fig-concept a, b). This would imply that knowing the general patterns and trends in community biomass in reponse to global change drivers could be used to predict the changes in plant biodiversity, without having to identify and test the direct effects of all the different drivers on mechanisms in each specific case. Furthermore, the magnitude of change in community biomass could serve as a proxy for the intensity of the effect of these global change drivers on biodiversity.

We hypothesize that climate warming, nitrogen addition, and grazing affect diversity and species composition via impacts on community biomass. Specifically, we expect warming and nitrogen addition to increase community biomass, leading to an increase in the intensity of competition for light and nutrients, and hence an increase in competitive exclusion. Grazing should have the opposite effects. Alternative mechanisms independent of plant-plant competitive interactions are also possible. For example, climate warming may shift conditions beyond or into the climate niche of some species, which may therefore go locally extinct or successfully colonise [@nomoto2021drivers]. Second, increased nitrogen addition, especially at high levels, can lead to soil acidification [@tian2015global], which can lead to shifts in species composition and diversity due to differences in tolerance to acidic conditions. Similarly, some species may have traits that make them particularly tolerant or intolerant to direct effects of grazing [@archibald2019unified], leading to community shifts not mediated through biomass. To further aid the interpretation of shifts in composition, and diversity, we use ecological indicators of species' responses to the environmental conditions [@diekmann2003species; @rumpf2018range], and calculate community weighted mean indicator values to provide further insights into the potential mechanisms underlying these dynamics.

To test the generality of biomass as a mediator of indirect global change effects, we conducted multi-factor global change experiments, along an elevational gradient in mountain grasslands (@fig-methods). Mountains harbor unique biodiversity and are subjected to multiple global change drivers [@dainese2024global; @Humbert2016-wg; @verrall2020alpine]. In addition, plant community responses to global change drivers often vary along environmental gradients and across habitats [@milchunas1993quantitative; @elmendorf2012plot; @Humbert2016-wg; @bjorkman2018plant; @Vandvik2020-hu] thus making elevational gradients an ideal natural laboratory to study global change impacts [@tito2020mountain]. We therefore manipulate three common global change drivers in a field experiment: climate warming, nitrogen deposition, and clipping or natural grazing, and replicated these experiments in an alpine and sub-alpine grassland community in Western Norway (@fig-methods). To simulate warmer climate, plant communities were transplanted to lower elevation. We further fertilised the communities using nitrogen levels ranging between 0 and 100 kg N ha^-1^ y^-1^, and simulated grazing effects by comparing clipping at two different intensities and natural grazing to a grazing exclosure treatment. After three years of global change treatments, we harvested community biomass and assessed the change in vascular plant species composition and diversity.
